opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I think about it a lot. For me, the prosperity of a research field isn't really measured by the number of papers published or how many citations people get. Those are lagging indicators, and sometimes they can even be misleading, because a field can be very busy without making real progress.

I'd look at a few things instead. First, are people able to build on each other's work quickly? When a field is healthy, a new idea comes out, and within weeks or months you see others extending it, combining it with something else, applying it to a problem nobody expected. That kind of compounding is a strong signal. In generative AI over the past several years, we've seen exactly that. Diffusion models, transformers, large-scale pretraining all fed into each other really fast.

Second, I'd ask whether the research is starting to touch the real world. Not every piece of research needs to be immediately useful, of course, but over time a prosperous field should create capabilities people actually use. For example, in my own area, world models and physical AI, the question is whether these models can eventually help robots learn, help autonomous vehicles be safer, help creators make things they couldn't before. When research starts to change what people can do, that's prosperity in a deeper sense.

Third, I think talent is a very important measure. Are young, smart people excited to come into the field? Are students choosing it because they see open problems that matter? If the best people want to work on something, that usually tells you there's still a lot of room to grow.

And finally, I'd say the number of good open questions matters. A field that's prospering keeps generating new questions faster than it answers the old ones. If everyone feels the main problems are solved and we're just tuning numbers on benchmarks, that's actually a sign the field might be saturating. But when every answer opens up three new questions, like what we're seeing now with physical AI, then you know it's a very exciting time to be doing research.

r001.rationale: It says a healthy field lets others build on a new idea within weeks or months, extending and combining it, which conveys how quickly ideas pass between researchers.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on what kind of research you're talking about, because there is no single number that captures it.

If you look at the traditional metrics—the number of papers, citations, how many submissions a conference like NeurIPS or CVPR gets—those tell you something, but mostly they tell you about activity, not about prosperity. A field can be very busy and still not be very healthy. When I was starting out, you could read almost everything in your area. Now there are so many papers that nobody can keep up, and a lot of them are incremental. So volume is not the measure I would use.

What I care more about is whether the research is actually changing what people can do. For me, the most meaningful signal is impact over a longer time horizon. Does an idea from five years ago show up in systems that people use today? When we worked on things like image-to-image translation or GAN-based synthesis, at the time it was mostly a research curiosity. The real measure came later, when those ideas became the foundation for generative models that are now in products and in tools that artists, engineers, and roboticists use every day. That is prosperity—when the boundary between research and practice gets thinner.

The second thing I look at is whether the field is producing people, not just papers. A prosperous research community trains students who go on to start new directions, new labs, new companies. If you look at who is doing the important work in generative AI or in physical AI today, many of them came out of a relatively small number of groups ten or fifteen years ago. That compounding of talent is more important than any single result.

The third thing, and this is maybe less obvious, is diversity of ideas. In a healthy field there are several competing approaches, and it's not clear which will win. Right now, scaling has been incredibly successful, and that's wonderful, but if everyone is only doing the same thing with more compute, the field becomes fragile. So I would measure prosperity partly by whether there is still room for a small group with a different idea to surprise everyone.

And finally, I think you have to ask whether research is connected to real problems. In my own area, we have moved from generating pretty images to asking how a model can understand physics, how a robot can learn from simulation, how you can build a world model that is actually useful for a self-driving car. The problems are getting harder and more grounded. To me, that is a sign that the field is growing up, not just growing.

So if I had to summarize: not how many papers, but how much the world's capability has changed, how many good people the field has produced, and whether there is still genuine intellectual diversity. Those are harder to count, but they are the ones that matter.

r001.rationale: The response measures prosperity through lasting real-world impact, talent development, intellectual diversity, and connection to practical problems. It does not propose measuring how quickly ideas pass from one person's mind to another's.

astra-6.text:
I think the prosperity of research should be measured by the progress it enables, rather than simply by the number of papers published. Are we asking important questions? Are we developing a deeper understanding? Can other researchers build on the results?

There’s also a longer-term dimension. Some research has an immediate practical impact, while some opens up a direction whose value only becomes clear years later. So I would look at both the impact of the work and the health of the research community—whether people have the freedom to explore, challenge assumptions, and pursue ideas that might fail.

r001.rationale: The response mentions whether other researchers can build on results, but it does not propose measuring prosperity by how quickly ideas pass between people.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the prosperity of research should be measured by the ideas it makes possible and the impact those ideas have, rather than simply by the number of papers published. Are we asking important questions? Are we discovering things that change how people think or enable them to solve problems they couldn’t solve before?

I would also look at the research community itself. Can young researchers pursue ambitious ideas? Is there room for approaches that might fail? Are people sharing knowledge and building on one another’s work? Some valuable research takes years to show its impact, so a healthy research environment needs both high standards and patience.

r001.rationale: The response mentions sharing knowledge and building on others’ work, but it does not propose measuring research prosperity by how quickly ideas pass between people.
